raw_comment:
1. I live in Milford, Delaware and I immediately searched for my county upon seeing the title of this graph. I noticed that I am particularly at risk for hurricanes, which--although we've had several--doesn't seem like it would be the most significant issue in my small state. I don't believe that we get nearly enough rainfall to be considered at risk for hurricanes.
2. Secondly, I wonder what this graph would correlate with. To elaborate, would states with higher sea level risks have more people who own boats? Or would people in CA--who are at risk for wildfires--be more likely to own a fire extinguisher compared to people who live in hurricane risk areas.
3. Finally, although this is completely irrelevant to the graph, I wondered why counties are shaped the way they are. The division of people into smaller classifications than states makes little to no sense to me, and the fact that there are counties in states like Nevada that are almost four times the size of my state boggles my mind.

raw_comment: My country is San Mateo County in California, USA. The thing that I noticed is the chart is a big threat which is Water Stress coming in first, our second threat would be Extreme Heat, and then our third is Extreme Rainfall. But the main issue I want to talk about when noticing would be Water Stress. Water Stress to me most likely is about our water quality, water shortages, and water scarcity, which is a lack of fresh water. I wonder if this threat will be settled in the near future, and if it doesn't will we ever find a way to have drinkable water? This will impact me and my community because everyday, some people drink water to either be dehydrated, to help our bodies, or just be pleased with their lunches with water. If there is no more water then the question is, what are we going to drink? We can't keep drinking sodas because they're made from carbonated water and carbonated water is made from water. It's possible to stay alive without drinking water for a few days most likely, but that wouldn't be more effective to us. In the graph, water stress is a serious threat and is probably going to happen to other countries soon. A catchy headline that I can think of is, "What's going on with our water supply?"

raw_comment: I live on the border of San Mateo County, the two biggest climate threats are high water stress and high sea level rise. The first thing I noticed is that though the charts are based on climate threats and what not, natural disasters are overlooked. Earthquakes are a big part of California’s disasters especially since the sea level is rising. Since San Mateo’s sea level and water stress is very high, earthquakes could enhance more natural disasters like tsunamis and flooding, Of course we can’t forget about the frequent wildfires that constantly ruin our environment and air quality. My only question is, if California is always in danger of droughts, why is the water stress so high? In California there is little to no rain, with the exception of rainy winters and snowy areas like Lake Tahoe. I do wonder if it’s because San Mateo is located on the border of the U.S where many oceans lie. Earthquakes, wildfires, and  flooding play a big factor in many homes here. Although it’s sad to say, San Mateo County is poor and many communities would not be able to recover from big disasters like these. The graph is a perfect representation of our biggest climate problems and exhibits what we can do to help our community move forward. I would title the graph, “How much danger are we really in?”

raw_comment: The first thing I did as many Americans did, I looked at my current home state. Once I looked at my home state (North Carolina) I see that we have almost every risk, with the exception of wildfires and water stress. As someone who  lives on coastal Carolina's, hurricanes are really common, though I guess 2020 felt bad and let up a little. The north east of the state is at risk of sea levels rising. More than half of the state is prone to hurricane risk. Then the western part of the state is prone to heavy rainfall. If you look very closely, the far west of the state is prone to heat stress. To add to that if you look and go from east to west, the colors change in order which I find really interesting. The colors shift from dark green, to light green, to dark blue, to light blue, or pale orange, to full orange. This could have something to do with the way the state goes from beaches to the Appalachian mountains, but I’m no expert.

raw_comment:
I notice that the map has color sections, meaning that most of the country is separated into risk sections; the west having wildfires & water stress, the midwest having extreme heat, and the east having extreme rainfall and hurricane risks. I also notice that the west and east have completely different climates. The west coast is prone to fires, heatwaves, and extreme rainfall. The east coast, on the other hand, is prone to extreme rainfall and hurricanes. Though they're obviously so different, they're not that far away, and it is fascinating how something only 3000 miles away can have a completely different climate. I wonder why most of the midwest suffers from droughts & water stress. Though it is expected with climate change, I wonder what exactly makes such a difference. I also wonder why some areas of the color "sections" have different climates mixed in them. Look at California, for instance. They have a small section of extreme rainfall risk, so I wonder why they have rainfall, of all things, next to wildfire risk. This has an extreme impact on me and my community. When wildfire season starts, there's definitely nerves within my community. Though we haven't burned yet, we get the worst of the smoke in our area. Some days we can't even go outside; the smoke is so pungent and in our face. A catchy title for this graph? 
"U.S. County Risks: Growing Larger By the Season".

In the meanwhile areas like Louisiana have dangers for extreme heat. To add on, I also notice, in the southeast, there is a chance of hurricanes occurring. As well in areas like Pennsylvania, they will most likely experience an enormous amount of rainfall. I wonder what might be the cause of this climate. raw_comment:

The impact on my community is that Essex county is expected to have high hurricane risk, medium water stress risk, medium extreme rainfall risk, medium sea level rise risk, low heat stress risk, and medium wildfire risk. 

I wonder how they made these predictions and what information it is based off of.

raw_comment: I notice that coastal states on the East Coast, along the Atlantic Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico, are at a heightened risk for hurricanes. Meanwhile, on the West Coast, the states are at risk for a variety of climate change effects, like water stress risk, wildfires, and extreme rainfall. I wonder how each of these conditions are related to one another. For example, extreme heat and water stress seem to go together, but in the Midwest, there’s a sudden shift from extreme rainfall to extreme heat. My county is at a high risk for hurricanes. While we thankfully haven’t experienced a hurricane directly impacting the Massachusetts coast, there has been an increase in hurricanes closer to the Gulf of Mexico. The remnants of the hurricane make their way up the coast until it impacts communities in New England as well, albeit at a smaller scale. A headline I would propose is, “The Silent Threat: The Real Impact of Climate Change."

raw_comment:
1. What do I notice?
What I notice is that certain areas around the U.S. have different climate threats depending on their location. As an example, more dry areas such as the Western part of the U.S. has a higher risk of water stress and wildfires. Meanwhile in the Eastern part of the U.S. and some of the Southern parts of the U.S. have more rain and storms, which makes them have a higher climate risk to hurricanes. 
2. What do I wonder?
Some things that I wonder about this graph is how are certain people with certain income affected in these counties? What I mean by this is that certain people who make more that $40K might have it better off than others who are below the poverty line. Yes, both sides will have to struggle during the events of the climate, however it is a guarantee that people who come with more wealth will be better off than others. Things such as the essentials are needed in a climate crisis, as an example in a state such as Arizona or Nevada, an essential during the event of a water stress would be water, and so people who are under the poverty line might not have access to those necessities.  
3.  The effects that a climate threat of hurricanes can have on my communities is that many people might have to go without power for weeks upon weeks considering that certain areas in Connecticut will be taken into more consideration rather than others. 
4. A title that would sum up the main idea of the map would be "The Climate Threats Among All of us."

I have also noticed that during the pandemic our earth has healed in some parts of the world due to less travel.

I wonder why in Arkansas there is a risk for extreme heat but some portions of the state are at risk for extreme rainfall. This map does not include bodies of water so that might be an explanation as to why there is a higher risk for rainfall in these areas. This impacts my community because I live in New Jersey and we are at a high risk for hurricanes which could seriously damage our state. raw_comment: I noticed that climate change has led to different parts of the country having different extreme risks. Most of the states on the East coast have a hurricane risk whereas many of the states on the West coast have a water stress risk. About half of California has a wildfire risk, which aligns with recent events. The risk that covers the most area would be water stress as it occupies the Midwest and parts of the West and South. However, since the Midwest is more sparsely populated compared to other parts of the country, I'm unsure that water stress affects the most people. I noticed states that are at risk for hurricanes or extreme rainfall are states that border or are very close to the water; landlocked states tend to be at risk for water stress or extreme heat. I wonder what specific factors of climate change cause each risk and which risks cause the most damage. I also wonder why most of Hawaii is at risk for extreme heat rather than sea level rise considering that Hawaii is a chain of islands. Similarly, I wonder what causes certain counties to be at a different risk compared to the rest of their state. My community is at risk for hurricanes, followed by extreme rainfall and water stress. This aligns with the weather that we experience. Even though we haven't experienced too many extreme weather conditions, it's a good reminder to show us we should still be wary of the weather and continue to monitor it. A headline could be Climate Change is Real: How is it Affecting You?

raw_comment:
I notice that the East will be dealing with a lot of wet weather, like rainfall and hurricanes. The west coast is the exact opposite with water stress and wildfires.The midwest leans more towards the weather in the west with extreme heat. However, in the Pacific Northwest the weather is wet and has increasing sea level, especially with Alaska. I see that climate change is amplifying a region's normal weather. 

I wonder how climate change can make some places colder and others hotter. How will these conditions worsen over time? How will these conditions affect people? I wonder whether other countries have such a diverse array of climate risks.

In my community, we have many smoky days in the fall. Some days are so bad that we are not allowed to go outside. With even more wildfire surrounding us, the number of days we have with raised AQI could increase and spread into the summer.

My title for the graph would be "Climate Change Is Crazy in the Counties of America".

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  “Could You Survive an Extreme Climate?  Well, You Might Just Be Living in One” by Max of Texas; “Nowhere Safe from the Effects of Climate Change” by Patrick from New York; "It Seems that the World is Divided Among the Parched and the Drenched" by Cooper of Durango, Colorado; “Mapping Out Climate Change “ by TES 8th Grade Science Class in Charlotte, North Carolina; and, "Is Your County at Extreme Risk for the Next Natural Disaster?" by Alyssa of Ohio.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Oct. 30 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who expects hurricanes in the fall but has been experiencing them in the summer, too, and James Bush of Pittsburgh, who appreciates the extreme rainfall for his garden, but not the flooding.

raw_comment: I notice that the east coast is at high risk for both rain and hurricanes, which makes sense due to the excess of water from the Atlantic Ocean and the size creates a perfect environment for hurricanes. The same is also true for most of the Pacific North West though because of the Pacific Ocean.  There is also a high fire risk in places that are known for droughts and often extreme heat, such as Arizona and Northern Califonia/South-Western Oregon. The areas with extreme heat stress risk are also clustered together and slowly disperse. I notice that Hawaii is in the middle of the Pacific Ocean has both high heat and sea-level rise risk. I also notice that Alaska has portions with high risk in all of the listed categories except for wildfires and hurricanes which I find interesting because Alaska is majorly coastal and has lots of forests. I also notice that northern Washington has high rainfall risk despite not being directly on the coast. I wonder if these results are recent especially the ones in California, with the most current ones started by a gender reveal party (it would probably be beneficial to stop having them as they can be very harmful and extremely are cis-normative). I wonder why there is water stress risk in  South Western California when it is coastal and not a portion of California as affected by wildfires. A good title that might work for this is "The World Should Be Worried About The Climate, Are You?".

raw_comment: Looking at the map — which shows the terrible conditions of the current United States— it’s easy to tell what the map is attempting to convey. It’s easy to notice that the map shows the effects of global warming on our country and how different areas —some with too much water and some with not enough— are being affected. As a student, I wonder what ideas have been brought up to combat this type of thing, could it be easy or hard for something so drastic in our country? The impact is widespread, for my area it contains extreme heat and an extreme rainfall risk. A great headline for this devastating map could be, “No, you aren’t looking at the fiery pits of hell, that’s only the United States climate”. The map immediately acknowledges a problem, one that needs to be addressed and figured out soon.

I noticed that the graph shows what is the greatest climate threat in each state and each county within that state. Most of the middle states have a high water stress while the states in the north/east suffer from extreme rainfall. I also noticed that states in the west coast can either suffer from wildfires or extreme wildfires which is interesting to note since they are the complete opposite.

I wonder why there are wildfires right next to areas with extreme rainfall such as Humboldt County California vs. Trinity County California. I also wonder if the states that are in the middle suffer from water stress because they don't have mass amount of water near them such as the coasts do. 

This impacts my community because when I selected my county in NJ it stated that we had a high hurricane risk. This makes sense as to why hurricanes/ tropical storms in the past have been so strong in our areas

A catchy headline for this graph could be: Color Coded Climate Change in Your County

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s map shows the greatest climate threats by U.S. county.  If you click on a county, you will see the six major threats evaluated for the county.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Keep noticing and wondering.  Stay tuned for next week’s graph about how pay varies with age for different jobs.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that almost every single county in the United States is affected by climate change in one way or another. The majority of US counties are at risk at impact from water stress. Some regions are affected by some risks more than others. For example, the California and Arizona regions are at great risk for wildfires while Florida is at a great risk for hurricanes. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder how much impact these climate threats have had on the United States’ communities already. Are some places still unaffected by them, but are at a high risk. Are some, like California, currently experiencing the consequences of these climate threats?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
As a resident of New Jersey, my community is most affected by the threat of hurricanes. Hurricanes have already been negatively impacted by the community in the past. For example, Hurricane Sandy destroyed property, and robbed people of their homes, leaving many homeless.

Write a catchy headline that captures the map’s main idea.
Be Careful of Climate Change: Greatest Climate Threats By County in the United States

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that almost every single county in the United States is affected by climate change in one way or another. The majority of US counties are at risk at impact from water stress. Some regions are affected by some risks more than others. For example, the California and Arizona regions are at great risk for wildfires while Florida is at a great risk for hurricanes. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder how much impact these climate threats have had on the United States’ communities already. Are some places still unaffected by them, but are at a high risk. Are some, like California, currently experiencing the consequences of these climate threats?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
As a resident of New Jersey, my community is most affected by the threat of hurricanes. Hurricanes have already been negatively impacted by the community in the past. For example, Hurricane Sandy destroyed property, and robbed people of their homes, leaving many homeless.

raw_comment:
Headline: Contrasting Climate Creates Calamity? Where is Our Country Headed?

I noticed that the climate across the US becomes wetter as you go east. In the west, wildfires plague the states due to dry conditions, and states in the middle of the country (not on the coast) are suffering due to water stress. Extreme heat hits the central-eastern parts, succeded by extreme rainfall and hurricanes near the coast. For Alaska, the sea level is rising, most likely due to ice in the north melting, and Hawaii's temperature is climbing steadily, possibly from the undersea volcanoes or from sunlight being absorbed by the ocean.

I wonder what the boundaries between certain climates are like. In the northern parts of California and Oregon, it shows that they are suffering from both extreme rainfal and wildfires. Head a little further east and there's water stress as well. Is it possible to have problems with all three of them in one state? I mean, wildfires and water stress I understand, but heavy rains should put out the wildfires and cure the water stress. It just seemed a little odd, is all.

raw_comment: This graph shows the different weather conditions across the United States. While the west coast is experiencing rainfall, wildfires, and water stress, the east coast has hurricanes and rainfall. On the other hand, the midwest is undergoing massive water stress, some extreme heat, and few parts of wildfires. I can infer that due to the many volcanoes that Hawaii includes, the weather has high heat stress. Within these categories, the severity in lighter or darker shades are shown in each county. For example, Shasta County displays darker red, meaning very high risk of wildfires. Neighboring it, is Lassen County showing a lighter shade to depict the lesser risk than Shasta. I wonder what occurred in Uvalde County in Texas to show high risk of wildfires. Why are there several counties in the mass of “extreme heat” showing high rainfall risk? The feature of searching a county and having it automatically highlighted is convenient. I was easily able to find my county and discover that we are experiencing high risk of wildfires and water stress. With the recent wildfires, our community was severely impacted. In addition to restrictions due to COVID, the fires added more concerns and security. The smoke made the air unhealthy which prevented sports and other outdoor activities. A catchy headline would be “Colors of the Weather.”

raw_comment:
Headline: Extreme weather differences across U.S.

This graph is showing the climate and conditions of places in the United States. For example, where I live in Humboldt County, there is extreme rainfall, but surrounding us there are wildfires covering lots of California.
I wonder why the west coast is burning with millions of acres of wildfires while the east coast is covered in extreme rainfall. I also wonder why Humboldt County and Del Norte County, California have extreme rain fall but the rest of California has water stress or wildfires. 
This doesn't impact my community very much because we are safe and have rainfall. Although, it does affect many people around my county because of the severe wildfire danger.
